A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VideoOrion and provide readable methods, equations, results, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across restructuring and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original video question-answering, referring, ablation, TemporalBench, and data-scaling results in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark results and ablations, including additional component comparisons, failure analyses, and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: The proposed two-branch architecture, RAM++ key-frame selection, GroundingDINO–SAM–XMem pipeline, object pooling/MLPs, prompts, and three-stage cross-entropy training remain. Newly tested component alternatives are ablation configurations; the default method is retained.

E1.justification: Section 3.4 and Table 1 add LLaVA-Video instruction data and an explicit egocentric QA dataset constructed from Ego4D and EgoExo4D, covering descriptive through deductive questions. Evaluation benchmarks remain unchanged; TemporalBench was already present in v1's appendix.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds LLaVA-OneVision. New Table 8 compares against models replacing the object branch with VideoMAE or UMT-L, introducing a substantive alternative representation comparison. Tables 6–7 also evaluate additional alternatives including Mask2Former, SAM2, and DINOv2-L.

E3.justification: Table 1 increases video instruction samples from 1.4M to 2.7M plus 1M egocentric samples, retaining one training epoch. New experiments introduce pipeline controls, token limits, and a 50-sample timing protocol. V2's blanket 765K Video-LLaVA ablation description differs from v1's specific 100K VideoChat2 subset disclosure for the pretraining ablation; unchanged scores do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: V2 adds systematic pipeline-component tests, DINOv2 and video-encoder comparisons, an object-only ablation, object-token-limit sensitivity, failure cases, and computational-cost analysis. These substantially expand investigation of design choices and practical limitations. The original attention case study and data-scaling analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without seed counts, repeated-training-run information, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. The new average runtime over 50 samples adds a measurement protocol, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces headline results under expanded training: VideoOrion's MVBench accuracy changes from 58.3 to 63.5 and Perception-Test from 53.4 to 65.2. VideoOrion+ TemporalBench results change from 20.7/60.4 to 20.3/61.8. Numerous new ablation and failure results are added, including runtime increasing from 8.27 to 11.46 seconds with the pipeline. Referring results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The tensor, mask-list, object-token, and key-frame selection definitions in Sections 3.2–3.3 are retained. Neither version supplies substantive theorems or proofs; expanded conceptual explanations do not introduce new formal reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract and central contributions retain the same scope: object-dynamics tokens, a detect–segment–track pipeline, and benefits for general video understanding and referring. V2's stronger descriptive language and additional evidence elaborate these existing claims.

C2.justification: V2 develops the earlier general limitations into concrete explanations of context compensating for missed objects and misplaced attention causing errors. It adds a language-alignment explanation for DINOv2's weaker results and discusses the measured 38.5% runtime overhead as a tradeoff. These materially expand mechanism and applicability discussions.

D1.justification: V2 adds egocentric QA construction details, identifies ChatGPT3.5 as the evaluator, and documents runtime. It omits v1's explicit resize-only treatment of object-branch frames and some projector details, including the two-layer LSTM specification. Main hyperparameters and hardware disclosures remain unchanged, with Table 8 becoming Table 13.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion broadens object-segmentation coverage to vision foundation models and tracking, adding works such as SAM2, TrackFormer, and ByteTrack, alongside new dataset and comparator citations. The central positioning relative to Chat-UniVi, Slot-VLM, and Artemis remains unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the introduction, related work, methodology, and experimental narrative. It consolidates projector and temporal-understanding analyses into the ablation section, moves TemporalBench from the appendix, and reorganizes the appendices. The author list also changes.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 6, 8, and 10–12 and failure Figures 6–7, expands the projector table, and restructures the training-data table. Existing figures and tables are resized or relocated, with revised captions and substantially reorganized appendix layouts. The retained scaling figure changes from Figure 6 to Figure 8.

improvement.justification: V1's pipeline choices and practical failure/cost limitations were weakly evaluated. V2 adds direct component and video-encoder comparisons, complementary-branch tests, failure analysis, and measured overhead, substantially strengthening validation and transparency. Expanded training prevents attributing the new headline scores solely to the method, and some ablation details become less clear, but the added evidence about the central design and its limitations provides a substantial net improvement.
